newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton urges progress on trade rows with Japan.
newsitem.headline: Clinton urges progress on trade rows with Japan.

text.p: President Clinton Sunday stressed the need to settle trade disputes with Japan over insurance and aviation that have bedevilled relations between the two economic powers.

Clinton told Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in a meeting on the fringes of a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders in Manila that the dispute over deregulation of Japan's insurance market was their most important two-way trade problem, a Japanese official told reporters.
But he also asked for Japan's help in promoting an issue on which Washington and Japan see eye-to-eye -- a U.S. plan to axe tariffs on information technology by the turn of the century.

Speaking to reporters after the meeting, Clinton said Hashimoto assured him of Japan's desire to settle their trade disputes. Clinton also said that economic recovery in Japan would help ease problems such as Japan's chronic trade surplus.

"I think insurance is the most important one right now," the Japanese official quoted Clinton as telling Hashimoto. Clinton said it was "important to achieve results" on insurance and to make progress on another thorny dispute over aviation.
Washington has pressed Japan in meetings on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference here to resolve the insurance dispute by a Dec. 15 deadline.

The dispute stems from U.S. charges that parts of the lucrative Japanese insurance market are closed to U.S. firms. The United States is opposed to Japn opening up a niche market for accident and health insurance, in which U.S. firms have a strong presence, before liberalising the wider market.
Clinton and Hashimoto also agreed to put their aviation talks on a higher level to speed a resolution of that dispute, the official said.
The disagreement centres on an aviation pact dating from the 1950s which Japan says favours the United States. The two sides have agreed to restart the aviation talks early next year.
